extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, IP policymakers, and practitioners assessing prior art
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining when a disclosure (printed, oral, public use, or via new media) qualifies as prior art for novelty and inventive-step/obviousness assessments, including jurisdictional variations and evidentiary rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art — availability to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify as a prior art disclosure the disclosure must be “available to the public”. In other words, it must (1) have become generally available without restriction to the members of the public; and (2) the person or persons receiving the document must have no special relationship to the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior art disclosure may consist of a printed publication, oral publication or public use. This principle is stated repeatedly (Canada summary, conclusion). Courts have phrased the test as “general availability without restriction” and “no inhibiting fetter”.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of the art / scope of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of the art comprises everything disclosed to the public in writing, verbally, by use or otherwise prior to the date from which the rights of priority belong to the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes publications, oral disclosures, public use and content of previously filed applications that have been published. Different jurisdictions may treat certain published applications differently for novelty vs inventive step (see related entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of disclosure (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aside from specific statutory/grace-period exceptions, the date when a disclosure occurred does not, in principle, affect whether something is prior art — a disclosure is a disclosure irrespective of how recent or old it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However courts have given less evidentiary weight to old prior art that was never put into practice (Canadian cases cited). Specific statutory exceptions (e.g., 6-month exhibition/evident abuse) or applicant-grace provisions modify timing effects in some jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional treatment of pending applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Pending (earlier-filed) patent applications that have been made available to the public may be part of the state of the art for novelty but, in many systems, are not decisive for inventive step/obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Danish law (and EPC practice) treats earlier-filed national/international/European applications made available to the public as state of the art for novelty but not for inventive step. Czech report: contents of such applications shall not be decisive for consideration of inventive step. Canadian summary: pending applications not yet published should not affect obviousness but should be citeable regarding novelty in first-to-file systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of disclosure — relevance and determination
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of novelty and inventive step the place of disclosure is generally not relevant; where it is determined, place should be the location of the persons viewing or receiving the prior art disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no special Canadian or Danish requirements limiting prior art by country. For internet disclosures, the disclosure should be considered to have occurred in the place from which it can be accessed (i.e. location of users), not the computer hosting the website.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of accidental vs intentional disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: It does not make a difference if a disclosure has occurred accidentally as opposed to intentionally — a disclosure remains a disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If accidental disclosures were excluded it would be impossible for third parties to determine patent validity. Some narrow statutory exceptions (e.g., evident abuse/exhibition) may apply in particular time windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicable law for determining whether disclosure occurred
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicable law for determining whether a disclosure has occurred is the law of the country in which novelty and inventive step are being assessed (e.g., Canada for Canadian proceedings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination follows domestic law; harmonization with EPC/EPO practice often influences national practice but the national law applies for that jurisdiction’s proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal elements — who disclosed and grace periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Different legal regimes provide different effects depending on who made the disclosure; some statutes grant grace periods for disclosures by the applicant (or persons who obtained knowledge directly or indirectly from the applicant) that differ from disclosures by third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canada: special grace periods for novelty depending on whether the applicant (or a person who obtained knowledge from the applicant) or a third party disclosed the subject matter. Denmark/EPC have 6-month exceptions for disclosures due to evident abuse or recognized exhibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of confidentiality or implied confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure that is made subject to restrictions of confidentiality or implied confidentiality will not be citeable as a prior art disclosure; conversely, some statements in the survey note that a disclosure in breach of a confidentiality agreement is nonetheless a disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tension in practice: courts require general availability without restriction for a publication to be citeable; at the same time some national commentary asserts that a disclosure is a disclosure even if the disclosing person was bound by confidentiality (with the patentee’s remedy being damages). The conclusion summary explicitly states that an accidental disclosure or a disclosure in breach of confidence are citeable prior art disclosures — but case law and practice may treat restricted disclosures as non-citable where confidentiality is established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of errors in disclosed information
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors in the disclosed information are generally not relevant — the important matter is the information conveyed to a person skilled in the art and his/her understanding of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denmark notes that obvious errors in a publication may be disregarded (case-by-case), e.g., incorrect figures in an abstract may be disregarded; otherwise a publication is valid as cited if meaningful to the skilled worker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient ability and skilled-person standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The test for whether a disclosure is a disclosure depends on what an ordinary person skilled in the art would be able to understand from the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oral information counts as disclosure if the persons receiving it understood it or could pass it on, even if the first recipients did not themselves fully understand. Printed publications give what a skilled worker can gain from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse engineering / disassembly as disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The possibility that a person might obtain the information through additional steps, such as disassembly of embodiments or reverse engineering, is sufficient to constitute a disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary to show that the product was actually dissected or reverse engineered; EPO guidelines and national cases support this (Baker Petrolite, Risi Stone cases referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperless / internet disclosures are prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no limitation on the nature of prior art disclosure; information communicated on electronic networks or the internet can constitute sufficient disclosure to affect novelty or inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have recognized oral and electronic disclosures as sufficient. No principled difference in standard, though practical evidentiary problems (establishing date, contents, access) make internet evidence harder to prove.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discoverability / diligent search requirement for internet disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: For internet disclosures to be relied on as prior art it must be demonstrated that the information would have been discovered by a person skilled in the art using appropriate search tools (i.e., discoverable by diligent search).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The internet disclosure must have been discoverable by means of a diligent search (e.g., via appropriate search engines or knowledge of particular websites). This is part of establishing public availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encryption, passwords, paywalls and public availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Encrypted information is not public unless it was disclosed to someone able to decrypt it and there are no restrictions; password-protected material may be public if the password can be acquired through a set, non‑discriminating procedure (payment akin to buying a magazine is not a bar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denmark: encryption -> not public unless decoding tool openly available; password access may still be public if readily acquirable; presence on search engines is not necessary for public availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence burden and standards for internet disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof for establishing a particular internet disclosure lies on the party relying on the prior art; internet evidence should be subjected to the same level of scrutiny as other types of disclosure evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts impose a heavy burden on parties alleging prior knowledge/use. Patent authorities/opponents relying on paperless information have responsibility to prove contents and publication date prior to filing. Start from publication date on page unless disputed; if manipulation is alleged, investigate.

rubrics_metrics.name: No different evidentiary levels by disclosure medium
rubrics_metrics.description: There should not be different levels of evidence for different ways of disclosure — since the legal impact (on novelty/obviousness) is the same, the standard of proof should be the same across media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although oral disclosure is less tangible, the standard applied should be the same regardless of the kind of disclosure; however oral disclosures often need corroboration by disinterested witnesses (case law cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration / archiving of internet disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no special statutory requirements for the duration of information on electronic means, but it is advisable that the information be available long enough to permit a diligent search, review and reproduction and that archiving be used to establish dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice: archives are highly desirable to establish availability date; while short-lived internet publications can still be prior art, availability long enough to be located/downloaded is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary weight of old, unused prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may give less evidentiary weight to old prior art that was never put into practice when assessing its significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canadian cases cited where age and lack of practical use reduced evidentiary weight (Creations 2000 Inc. v. Canper; Almecon Industries cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulation concerns for internet evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: As a starting point one should disregard the possibility of manipulation of internet content; however if manipulation is alleged, an investigation is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a party claims possible manipulation of web content or dates, patent authorities should investigate claims rather than treating internet evidence as inherently suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific exceptions — evident abuse and exhibition disclosures (six‑month rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some laws provide that a disclosure occurring not earlier than six months before filing will not be considered part of the state of the art if it was due to evident abuse in relation to the applicant or if the applicant displayed the invention at an officially recognized international exhibition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denmark and EPC-derived provisions referenced (Art. 55(1) EPC / Paris Convention). Czech report similarly notes a six-month exception where disclosure was due to evident abuse and the invention was displayed at a recognized international exhibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emails and private correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Emails are usually considered private and not public; private correspondence normally will not be treated as a public disclosure unless other conditions are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denmark notes that generally emails are private and non-public available correspondence and therefore not prior art unless other indicia of public availability exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonization and use of EPO guidelines as reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Many national offices align practice with EPO/EPC guidelines; in absence of national rules for new media, reference to EPO or other offices’ operational guidelines is common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denmark explicitly states it will comply with general EPO practice; paperless disclosure guidance may be informed by JPPTO Operational Guidelines and EPO Guidelines sections cited.
